Science teacher's note, Friday
For most of this term Imran, Class 9, has eaten lunch alone near the water tank. I have seen him try to join the cricket group twice; both times they closed ranks, without really meaning to.
Two weeks ago I put up a notice for the new astronomy club, meeting Tuesdays after school. Imran came to the first session and sat at the back. Vinita, from Class 10, was struggling to focus the old telescope. Imran quietly showed her how; he had watched videos about it for months. Since then the two of them have been the first to arrive, arguing happily about Saturn's rings.
Yesterday at lunch I saw him sitting with Vinita and three others from the club, sketching a star chart in a notebook.
Next step: I will ask Imran to help plan our moon-watching night.

qa.a: Tuesdays after school.

Today was the third week of garden club, and I think I actually like it.
Before this I spent every break hanging around the popular boys near the canteen. They'd laugh before I got to the end of my jokes, or just turn their backs. I'd go home feeling like a shadow.

Nobody here cares who's cool. We talk about soil and aphids and whose turn it is to water. At lunch Lavanya saved me a spot on the bench.
Tomorrow's my watering day. I've set an alarm.
Jagdish

My first winter in the Delhi hostel, I found a way not to feel lonely. Or I thought I had. After dinner I'd lie on my bed and scroll: cooking videos, strangers' vlogs, my school friends' photos from Guwahati. Urmila's birthday party. A picnic I wasn't at. Everyone laughing on a boat.
For an hour it felt warm, like sitting in a busy room. Then it would be 2 a.m., my eyes stinging, and the room would feel emptier than before. I'd see Urmila's message from Tuesday, "call when free?", still unanswered, because calling felt like effort and scrolling didn't.
The worst part was the comparing. Everyone else had a life; I had a screen with their lives on it.
I'm Neelam, and it took me most of that winter to notice the screen wasn't company. It was a window into rooms I wasn't in.

qa.q: What did Urmila's unanswered message say?
qa.a: Call when free?

qa.q: How did Neelam feel at 2 a.m. after scrolling?
qa.a: Neelam felt lonelier and emptier, eyes stinging, as comparison replaced the brief warmth.

qa.a: Called Urmila back, even briefly, since a real voice gives the warmth that watching others' photos doesn't.

Hostel warden's note, 3 October
Elizabeth, first year, from Kottayam, has spent most evenings in her room since mid-September. The night guard says her light and phone screen stay on past 3 a.m. At breakfast she sits alone, scrolling, and barely eats. Her roommate says she watches videos of her home church choir and her old school friends for hours.
When I stopped by this evening, she said, "It's fine, ma'am. It's like being home for a bit." Then her eyes filled. She said it helps while she watches and feels worse afterwards, because everyone back home seems to be going on without her.
I did not lecture her about phones. I told her many first-years feel this, and that I was glad she told me. Vikas, our student floor mentor, will invite her to Friday movie night in the common room, and I have given her the college counsellor's hours in case the low feeling doesn't lift.

qa.a: Past 3 a.m.

qa.q: What did Elizabeth feel when her eyes filled?
qa.a: She felt homesick and lonely, the videos giving brief comfort but leaving her feeling left behind.

Swati, you've been hiding in your room since you came home. I was you at twenty.
It was my second year at college in Shillong. Slowly I stopped going to the canteen, then to class. I slept all day and lay awake all night. My appetite vanished. She put on her shawl, took my hand and walked me straight to the warden's room that same night. The warden phoned my father, and next morning took me to the college doctor.
That walk down the corridor was the turning point. So let me be your Daphi tonight. I'm Arohi, your old aunt, and I'm listening.

Sonali had been in Pune six months for her job, and in that time she had spoken to exactly nobody outside the office. Tonight the monsoon had knocked out the power in her building, her laptop was dead, and the flat was so quiet she could hear the neighbour's fridge.
With nine per cent battery left, she opened a chat she hadn't touched since college: Alka. The last message was from Alka, eight months old. "Miss you, idiot."
Sonali typed and deleted three times. Too long. Too sad. Too weird. Finally she sent: "Power cut here. Thought of you. How are you?"
She put the phone face down and made tea by candlelight, heart thumping as if she had asked someone to dance.
Four minutes later the phone buzzed. "SONALI! I thought you'd vanished. Call me right now before your battery dies."
She laughed out loud in the dark.

qa.q: What did Sonali finally send?
qa.a: Power cut here. Thought of you. How are you?

qa.q: How did Sonali feel after sending the message?

For his first months there, every evening went the same way: he climbed onto the roof of his rented room, where the network was best, and scrolled until midnight, watching friends in Ranchi at cafés and weddings.

So he made a rule. Phone on the roof from eight to nine, not after. And one real thing every day: a call to his mother, a chat with the tea-stall owner, carrom with the headmaster's son.
On Sundays he now called Mridul, his college friend, for a proper hour instead of sending him reels. Last week Mridul said, "You sound like yourself again."

passage:
In her tiny flat in south London, Amara had been spending every evening in bed with her phone, watching strangers cook, travel and fall in love. By the time she looked up it was one in the morning, and she felt emptier than when she'd started.
In January she made a deal with herself. Social apps only between seven and eight, timer on. And every day, one offline thing, even a small one.
Monday she called her grandmother in Lagos. Tuesday she asked Jin, her flatmate, whom she'd barely spoken to in months, if he wanted to cook jollof together. Jin burned the onions; Amara laughed until she cried. Wednesday they walked to the market. Thursday Jin taught her a card game from Busan.
She still watched cooking videos. But now, some nights, she cooked the recipes with someone.

qa.q: When does Amara allow herself social apps?
qa.a: Only between seven and eight, timer on.

qa.q: How did Amara feel at one in the morning before the change?
qa.a: She felt empty and lonely after hours of watching strangers' lives.

qa.q: Why does pairing screen time with an offline plan help?
qa.a: It keeps the phone a tool and adds real contact, like cooking with Jin, that screens can't replace.

qa.q: What might Jin feel when Amara asks to cook together?
qa.a: Jin is probably surprised and pleased, glad to finally connect with a flatmate he barely knew.

grounding: A young woman sets a window for apps and pairs it with a daily offline plan, turning a flatmate into real company.

passage:
When Ma'am said, "Spelling test after the break," Rashmi's stomach twisted into a tight knot. Her heart thumped so hard she could feel it in her ears.
She looked at Aadhya, who was humming and swinging her legs. How could she be so calm? Something bad must be coming. Rashmi's hands went cold and sweaty at the same time.
At break she didn't eat her paratha. She sat on the bench and whispered the words again and again: necessary, necessary. The letters kept jumbling.
"Are you sick?" Aadhya asked.
"I think so," Rashmi said. Her tummy hurt so much, it must mean the test was dangerous somehow. That's what it felt like. Like a dog about to bite.

qa.q: What did Rashmi not eat at break?
qa.a: Her paratha.

qa.q: Why did Rashmi think the test must be dangerous?
qa.a: She felt so scared, with a knotted stomach and thumping heart, that her body's alarm seemed like proof of danger.

qa.q: What could help Rashmi in this moment?
qa.a: A teacher or parent could explain that the knot is her body's alarm, not a sign of danger, and help her take slow breaths.

qa.q: What might Aadhya think when Rashmi says she might be sick?
qa.a: Aadhya may be puzzled and a little worried, not knowing how frightened Rashmi feels about the test.

grounding: Before a spelling test a child's stomach knots and heart thumps, and the body's alarm feels like proof that something is truly dangerous.

grounding: A young boy's pounding heart and shaking legs at the sight of a sleeping dog feel to him like proof of real danger.

passage:
On my first day at the new school in Dehradun, I stood outside Class 5B and my stomach tied itself in a knot. My heart was banging like someone knocking on a door. I thought, this means something bad will happen in there.
Inside, thirty faces turned to look at me. My ears went hot. I wanted to run back to the gate, where Amala was still waving.
The teacher said, "Tenzin, sit next to Madhav." Madhav moved his bag and smiled. I didn't smile back. I was too busy holding my stomach.
Nothing bad happened that day. Madhav shared his eraser. But I still remember how sure I was, standing at that door, that my thumping heart knew something I didn't.

qa.q: Who did the teacher ask Tenzin to sit next to?
qa.a: Madhav.

qa.q: What did Tenzin believe the banging heart meant?
qa.a: Tenzin felt scared and believed the body's alarm meant something bad would happen inside the class.

qa.q: What could a parent or teacher tell Tenzin before a first day?
qa.a: That a knotted stomach and fast heart are normal alarms in new places, not proof of danger, and that they usually settle.

qa.q: What might Madhav have felt when Tenzin didn't smile back?
qa.a: Madhav may have felt a bit unsure, but kept being friendly by sharing an eraser.

grounding: A child's knotted stomach and banging heart at a new class feel like proof that something bad is about to happen.

passage:
Every Thursday was swimming class at the club pool, and every Thursday morning Ramesh's stomach began to hurt at breakfast.
"Amma, my tummy," he said this Thursday, holding his side.
Irawati felt his forehead. No fever. But his face was pale, so she said, "Fine, stay home today."
The moment she said it, the ache melted. Ramesh felt light, as if a heavy school bag had been lifted off his back. He spent the morning building a block tower and humming.
The next week, the ache came on Wednesday night, right after dinner. By bedtime he was curled up, sure he couldn't go.
Irawati sat on the edge of his bed, frowning. The ache was real; she could see it. But it seemed to know exactly what day it was.

qa.q: What day was swimming class?
qa.a: Every Thursday.

qa.q: How did Ramesh feel when his mother said he could stay home?
qa.a: He felt a huge relief, as if a heavy bag had been lifted, and the ache melted away.

qa.q: What could Irawati try before next Thursday?
qa.a: Stay calm and kind about the ache, talk to the swimming teacher, and help him go for part of the class so avoidance doesn't grow; if the ache keeps going or worries her, check with the doctor.

qa.q: What is Irawati noticing as she sits on his bed?
qa.a: She notices the ache is real but always arrives before swimming, and feels puzzled and worried.

grounding: A child's stomach ache lets him skip swimming, the fear drops at once, and the next week the ache starts even earlier.

"It's... better now. A bit."
"Just like that?"

Sonali sat down on the bed. "Devu, what do you think will happen next Monday?"
"My tummy will hurt on Sunday night," Devika said in a small voice. "Even earlier."

qa.a: The dance practice for Annual Day.

qa.q: Why did Devika's tummy feel better so quickly?
qa.a: She felt a rush of relief when told she could stay home, which made the fear and the ache drop at once.

qa.q: What could Sonali and Mumma do before next Monday?
qa.a: Talk gently with Devika's teacher about the dance, and help her go for a short part of practice so the fear shrinks instead of growing.

qa.q: What might Sonali be feeling as she sits on the bed?
qa.a: Sonali feels caring but uneasy, seeing the Monday pattern and worried it will get worse.

grounding: A girl's tummy ache keeps her home from dance practice, the fear vanishes at once, and she senses it will start earlier next time.

qa.a: Tarun might believe it and just feel sorry, not knowing the real fear behind it.

grounding: A child who stayed home from an assembly task felt instant relief, and now the stomach ache starts days earlier.

After Tushar froze during the district debate in Sehore, with the whole school watching, he told himself he'd simply skip debates from now on.
But the avoiding spread. He stopped answering the landline, in case a relative asked about the debate. He stopped going to the vegetable market for his mother, because people there knew him. When his friends shouted from the lane for cricket, he pretended to be asleep. Last week he even let the tuition teacher's call ring out.
Each time he felt relief, like a door closing on a cold wind. And each time the next thing seemed a little scarier.
Parveen didi from next door found him on the roof on Sunday. "You used to be everywhere in this mohalla," she said. "Now I only see you up here."
Tushar shrugged. The world below looked noisy and sharp, and the roof felt like the only safe place left.

qa.q: Where did Tushar freeze?
qa.a: During the district debate in Sehore.

qa.q: What does Tushar's relief each time he avoids something show?
qa.a: He feels anxious, and the relief makes avoiding feel safe, so the fear spreads to more and more things.

qa.q: What could help Tushar at this stage?
qa.a: Starting with small steps back, like one market errand with his mother, and telling a trusted adult how scared he feels.

qa.q: How does Parveen didi see the change in Tushar?
qa.a: She is surprised and concerned, missing the boy who used to be everywhere in the mohalla.

grounding: After freezing at a debate, a teen avoids the phone, errands and friends, and each relief makes the world feel more threatening.

After Mei's voice cracked during her class presentation in Singapore, she decided she would just stay quiet in class for a while.
But the quiet grew. She muted the class group chat. She stopped going to the hawker centre after school with the others, in case Tariq brought up the presentation. When her phone rang, even with her aunt's name on the screen, her chest tightened and she let it go to voicemail. On Saturday she skipped the badminton club she had loved since primary school.
Each time she felt a quick flood of relief. Then, a little later, the next thing felt harder.
Tariq caught her at the lockers on Monday. "Hey, the group project's on Thursday. You'll come?"
Mei's heart raced. "Maybe. I'll see."
She knew she wouldn't. Her world was getting smaller, and everything outside it felt sharper every week.

qa.q: What club did Mei skip on Saturday?
qa.a: The badminton club she had loved since primary school.

qa.q: What does Mei's racing heart at Tariq's question show?
qa.a: She feels anxious and trapped, as even a simple invitation now feels threatening.

qa.q: What could Mei try before Thursday?
qa.a: Tell Tariq or a trusted adult honestly about the fear, and go to the group project for at least part of the time.

qa.q: What might Tariq notice about Mei?
qa.a: Tariq may notice her pulling away and feel puzzled or worried, not knowing it started with the presentation.

grounding: After one shaky presentation a teen avoids chats, outings, calls and her club, and her circle of safe activities keeps shrinking.
